plan.rationale: The question asks both "how much comes back" and "where", so the headline pricing is cut by payer and denial type together, with single-cut recovery rates behind it to show which side of that interaction is doing the work. The two contrasts name the strongest and weakest ends with a test, and the timeliness curve plus the deadline split are the standing levers the reader can actually act on.

report.narrative: Priced by payer and denial type: each population's open denials at that population's own measured rate. Every rate here is measured on your own denials. Nothing is filled in from an industry average. $2,430,765.30 — 42.3% of the open denied dollars — sits in 26 populations your own history cannot price yet, and is left out of the figure above. Rates here are measured over the 2,533 denials the payer has already answered, out of 5,398 denials in this population. 212 denials have been resubmitted and are still waiting on the payer. They are counted in neither the wins nor the losses. 2,653 denials have no resubmission on file. Some of those have not been worked yet rather than never; nothing in the data separates the two. Everything above is as the data stood on Aug 2, 2026. Of the open denials your own history can price, the expected recoverable dollars come to **$1,167,668.88** (F1) — measured directly against $5,749,495.12 of open denied dollars spread over 2,865 open denials (F1). The range around that total runs from a lowest the recoverable dollars could be of $874,052.42 to a highest of $1,518,693.69 (F1); because it is built by summing each population's own range, and populations that share payers, staffing and seasons move together, read it as a spread rather than a guarantee. Reconciliation is not applicable on this answer. On where the money sits, the payer spread runs from a strongest payer recovering 56.8% of the 148 denials it has answered to a weakest payer at 29.1% of 117 answered — a gap of 27.7 points, itself falling somewhere between 15.8 and 38.4 points (F4, measured directly). By denial type the spread is far wider: 62.2% at the strong end on 508 answered denials against 3.0% at the weak end on 66 answered, a gap of 59.2 points bounded between 50.7 and 63.8 points (F5, measured directly). Both pairs were picked precisely because they sit at the ends of the range, so each gap is a place to look rather than a result that has been confirmed (F4, F5). The $2,430,765.30 across 26 populations that no rate could price (F3, measured directly) is an inventory of denied dollars awaiting enough answered history — the dollars are counted and shown, but no rate stands behind them, so nothing there should be read as a forecast of what they would return. Timing is the other axis the money divides on. Of the open denied dollars, $2,831,002.86 are still inside the filing deadline and $2,918,492.26 are past it, with nothing sitting on plans with no limit on file (F2, measured directly) — that is a position count, not a statement that the past-deadline dollars are lost. What the deadline is worth shows up in the rates themselves: inside the filing deadline, denials recover at 44.6% where the limit needs confirming and 42.9% where it is confirmed, against 7.5% and 0.0% respectively past it (F7, measured directly). Speed of work tracks the same direction, with a 54.4% recovery rate when resubmitted fastest versus 14.2% when resubmitted slowest (F6, measured directly). Read together, the priced total (F1) is best understood as what the answerable portion of the inventory supports at your own measured rates, with the strongest concentration of upside where a high-recovering denial type (F5) or payer (F4) still sits inside the filing deadline (F2, F7) and can be worked quickly (F6) — and with the unpriced populations (F3) left outside that arithmetic entirely rather than assumed to be worth nothing.
context_notes: Getting the work out inside 0-14 days is worth 40.1 percentage points on the recovery rate compared with the slowest group.
Clinical / medical necessity denials currently take a median of 31 days to go back out.
Coding denials currently take a median of 9 days to go back out.
Final — non-appealable denials currently take a median of 49 days to go back out.
Registration and eligibility denials currently take a median of 13 days to go back out.
Routing and coordination of benefits denials currently take a median of 20 days to go back out.
The drop is steeper where the filing limit is confirmed than where it is still a planning default, so the two are shown apart. Treating every limit as confirmed overstates the cliff.
None of the 39 answered denials filed past a confirmed deadline came back. That is not the same as never: on this many denials the true rate could still be as high as 9.0%.
Clinical denials rest on medical necessity and need documentation, not a correction — they are worked more slowly and won less often.
Coding denials are usually correctable — a modifier, a code pair, or a unit count that can be fixed and sent back.
Registration and eligibility denials usually trace to demographics or coverage captured at the front end, and are correctable once the right coverage is found.
Routing and COB denials usually mean the claim went to the wrong payer or in the wrong order; the fix is a rebill to the right one.
